explain.summary: When Mateo scrapes his knee, tiny pieces in his blood called platelets rush to the broken vessels and stick together like glue. Thread-like fibrin holds them in a plug, so the bleeding slows minute by minute and stops on its own — even under a bandage. The plug dries into a scab while new skin grows underneath.
rules: Bleeding halves every so many minutes as the plug builds.
A bigger scrape takes longer to halve; fewer platelets take longer too.
Pressing on it makes the bleeding stop sooner.
Plug strength rises as the bleeding falls.

source.fact: Bleeding from small skin vessels normally stops within 1 to 9 minutes; low platelet counts make it take longer.
Platelets help blood clot; a normal count is 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter.
Platelets stick together to make a clot held by thread-like fibrin; it dries into a scab, new skin grows underneath, and the scab falls off after a week or two.

choice.what: Bleeding halves at a steady rate
choice.why: A halving curve fits 'fast at first, then slower' and stops within the 1–9 minute range for the default scrape.

choice.what: Platelet count scales the time directly
choice.why: Fewer platelets means a slower plug; the real relationship is more complicated.
Pressing helps; the exact amount varies, so we picked a clear but modest effect.

illustrative: Mateo's scrape size, his platelet count (250,000) and the 5-minute stop are made up for a fictional story.
Bleeding is shown as a percentage of the first minute, not in millilitres.

citations.title: Bleeding time
citations.supports: Bleeding time measures how fast small blood vessels in the skin stop bleeding; bleeding normally stops within 1 to 9 minutes; low platelet counts can make it take longer.

citations.title: Platelet count
citations.supports: Platelets are particles in the blood that help it clot; a normal count is 150,000 to 400,000 per microliter.

citations.title: What's a Scab?
citations.supports: Platelets stick together like glue to make a clot, held together by thread-like fibrin; the dried clot becomes a scab; new skin cells grow underneath; the scab falls off after a week or two.

does: Shows bleeding slowing and stopping on its own as a plug forms
Shows bigger scrapes taking longer and pressing helping
Shows that the plug needs platelets, not air
doesnt: Measure any real cut or anyone's real platelet count
Include germs, cleaning a wound or how deep a cut is
Show the week of healing under the scab
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: A cut that won't stop bleeding after you press on it for 10 minutes, or one that is deep, is a reason to tell an adult right away.
